Blood is a mixture of cellular components suspended in a liquid called plasma. The total volume of circulating blood represents 8% of the body weight, with plasma representing 55% of this volume. Blood serves as a carrier for the cardiovascular system.

The blood performs several functions: - delivery of O2 and substances absorbed by the digestive tract to the cells - transport of CO2 to the lungs and metabolic waste to the kidneys. - transport of hormones to their target organs. - maintenance of body temperature, blood pH and adequate volume of fluid in the circulatory system. - prevention of hemorrhages

1- PLASMA - yellowish liquid, slightly viscous - composed of 90% water and solutes (nutrients, gases, hormones, products and waste of cellular metabolism, ions and proteins, 60% of which are represented by albumin. The composition of plasma varies according to cellular activity. The concentrations of solutes are maintained at physiological values ??thanks to readjustments carried out by several organs (liver, kidneys, lungs, etc.).
2- FIGURED ELEMENTS or cellular elements suspended in plasma, represented by: - ??leukocytes or white blood cells - erythrocytes or red blood cells or red blood cells - platelets
Erythrocytes do not contain a nucleus, and almost no organelles. Platelets are cellular fragments.

2- FIGURED ELEMENTS Hematopoiesis is the formation of blood cells which takes place in the bone marrow. The figured elements have a common origin despite their different functions. They are produced from an undifferentiated stem cell, the hemocytoblast, located in the red bone marrow, also called a pluripotent hematopoietic stem cell.
2- FIGURED ELEMENTS Erythrocytes transport blood gases thanks to hemoglobin, a red ferroprotein, giving the blood its color.

The production of erythrocytes is called erythropoiesis. 2 to 3 million GR/second are produced by our body. Their lifespan is 100 to 120 days. The normal erythrocyte count is on average 5.4 x 1012/l in men and 4.8 x 1012/l in women.
Elaine N Marieb-Katja HoehnHuman Anatomy and PhysiologyAdapted from the 8th American edition
2- FIGURED ELEMENTS Leukocytes are represented by: - ??neutrophils: 50% of WBC - lymphocytes: 25% of WBC - monocytes: 3 to 8% of WBC - eosinophils: 2 to 4% of WBC - basophils: 0.5 to 1% of WBC
Leukocytes = 4.8 to 10.8 x 109 /l of blood. Function: protection of the body against bacteria, viruses, parasites, toxins and tumor cells. Lifespan: 0.25 to 9 days.
Elaine N Marieb-Katja HoehnHuman Anatomy and Physiology
Platelets or megakaryocytes or thrombocytes play an essential role in blood clotting. Shelf life: 10 days Platelets: 150 to 350 x 109/l of blood.
Elaine Nmarieb-Katja HoehnHuman Anatomy and PhysiologyAdapted from the 8th American edition

Hemostasis includes all the phenomena that allow bleeding to stop. It is done in 3 stages: - the vascular stage - the platelet stage - coagulation. Vascular time and platelet time constitute primary hemostasis.

- immediate but transient reflex vasoconstriction of the small vessels which have been damaged - adhesion test of the damaged endothelial cells. - closely linked to the platelet phase which follows it.
3- PLATELET TIME: formation of a platelet nail or white nail: - adhesion of platelets to subendothelial collagen

under the effect of Willebrand factor, leading to significant morphological changes: the platelets become spherical, emit pseudopodia, with a toothed wheel outline, and secrete the contents of their granules. The adhesion of the platelets therefore leads to their activation. - platelet secretion or Release phenomenon

5- FIBRINOLYSEFibrinolysis: - follows coagulation - ensures repermeabilization of the vessel. - is preceded by retraction of the clot in 1 to 4 hours, then lysis of the latter by crumbling in 48 hours. It results from the activation of plasminogen into plasmin under the effect of a tissuee factor produced by endothelial cells: t-PA. Plasmin degrades fibrin by producing PDFs (fibrin degradation products).

6- FUNCTIONAL EXPLORATION - Exploration of the vascular time - Bleeding time: - Duke method: normal: 3 to 4 min - Ivy method: Normal: 4 to 8 min - lying down in vascular anomalies, platelet anomalies and Willebrand factor anomalies. - Assessment of capillary resistance: yaw or suction cup sign.
- Exploration of platelet time - Bleeding time (TS) - Platelet count: 150,000 to 300,000/mm3
If < 100,000/mm3: thrombocytopenia If > 400,000/mm3: hyperplateletosis - Platelet quality test - Measurement of platelet functions - Retraction of the clot - Lifespan of platelets

- Exploration of coagulationExploration of the endogenous pathway - Clotting time: normal plasma in contact with the wall of the tube. Coagulation takes place in 5 to 8 min. - Howell time: plasma recalcification time; it is 2 to 3 min. - Active partial thromboplastin time (ACT) (or TCK): - plasma (patient) + partial thromboplastin + Ca2+ . - explores the endogenous pathway (XI,XII, IX,VIII,
Exploration of the exogenous pathway - Prothrombin time (PT) - plasma (patient) + thromboplastin + Ca2++

- explores the exogenous pathway (VII, X) + common pathway (V, II, I) - it is 12 to 14 s - pathological if > 2 s /control - generally converted into a percentage of activity compared to a pool of normal or reference plasma, which corresponds to 100%. It is called prothrombin level. It is between 70 and 100%.

- Exploration of fibrinoformation - Thrombin time: plasma coagulation time in the presence of diluted thrombin. It is 15 to 20 s, pathological if > 5 s/control. - Reptilase time: thrombin is replaced by reptilase. - Dosage of fibrinogen: 2 to 4 g/l.

-Exploration of fibrinolysis - Euglobulin lysis test or Von Kaulla test: - measures the time required for the dissolution of a clot - Normally > 3 h - pathological if < 3 h - determination of PDFs (fibrin degradation products) - Dosage of D-dimers (fibrin specific PDFs) - Dosage of t-PA, PAI (t-PA inhibitor), plasmin, plasminogen

Abnormalities of fibrinoformation: - fibrinogen dosage - thrombin time: if prolonged: taking anticoagulants or dysfibrinogenemia hence the need to take the reptilase time. - Reptilase time: If prolonged thrombin time and normal reptilase time: taking anticoagulants (heparin) If prolonged thrombin time and prolonged reptilase time: dysfibrinogenemia
